Lab 004 · Lessons 004–006 · measured live on your device

Cache Lab

A real particle pool, updated every frame. Lesson 004: same particles, same code, only the order of the reads changes. Lesson 005: same particles, same work, only the layout in memory changes. Lesson 006: same particles, same work, only the order of rain and blood changes, and the CPU has to guess. Watch what each does to the time.

Rain and blood particles, night city level. Goal: 500,000 particles, at least 10 seconds played, and the loop still reads memory in order.

          Profiler capture: particle modules
          
    
          Each module is timed on its own, every frame (median of the last 40 frames). "Loaded" counts the bytes the module pulls in from memory: whole 64-byte cache lines. "Used" counts the bytes it actually needs. Recycle is different: it jumps to each dead particle and moves the last particle into its place, so we count the cache lines it touches per dead particle.

          Order test
          
      
    
          
    
          The same update loop, time frozen, at four sizes. Each size runs twice: reads in slot order, and reads in a fully shuffled order. It takes about 10 seconds; the live view pauses while it runs. Watch the last column jump once the data no longer fits in your CPU's caches.

          What this shows
          
    
          
      
          Order is a cost
          The same 500,000 updates take several times longer when each read jumps somewhere new. Nothing in the code got slower. The memory did.
          
      
          Size decides how much
          When the data fits in the caches (20K particles is 640 KB), a shuffled order costs little. When it doesn't fit, every jump is a trip to RAM.
          
      
          Containers decide order
          A free list scrambles the order on its own within seconds. Swap-and-pop keeps the live particles packed, so the loop always reads front to back.
          
    
          
    
          Lesson 005 · data layout
          
    
          
      
          Loaded is not used
          The CPU always loads whole 64-byte lines. With one big struct, the Age module loads 64 bytes to use 4. That is 94% wasted trips to memory.
          
      
          Lay data out by how it is read
          With arrays of fields, every byte a module loads is a byte it needs. The work is the same; the bytes the modules load drop from 128 MB to 22 MB per frame.
          
      
          Splitting has a price
          With 16 arrays, removing one particle touches 16 cache lines instead of 1. Grouping fields that are always read together (pos with vel, rot with spin) keeps the streams 100% useful and cuts that to about 5.
          
    
          
    
          Lesson 006 · branches and SIMD
          
    
          
      
          An if is a guess
          The CPU doesn't wait to see which way an if goes. It guesses and keeps working. A wrong guess throws that work away. With rain and blood mixed at random, half the guesses are wrong.
          
      
          Order decides the cost
          Same particles, same work. Sorted or in a steady pattern, the guesser is almost never wrong. Random, it is wrong about half the time, and Fade gets several times slower.
          
      
          No jump, then 8 at once
          Branchless code computes both answers and picks one: no guess. With no jump inside, the compiler can use SIMD and do 8 particles per instruction. Splitting rain and blood into their own arrays removes the if completely.
          
    
          
    
          Lesson 006 mode: the if / else, branchless and split loops are real JavaScript, timed live with performance.now() on 500,000 particles (time frozen, so only Fade runs). JavaScript has no SIMD, so the "+ SIMD" version can't be measured here; its device time shows "—" and the laptop model gives the lesson's number. "Wrong guesses" come from a small guesser model (a table of 2-bit counters indexed by the last 8 outcomes), run over the real kind array; real CPUs use bigger, smarter guessers, but they can't guess random data either. The laptop numbers are the lesson's model, not measurements.
          
    
          Measured live with performance.now(): this is the real loop, in JavaScript, on your device. A particle is 8 floats (32 bytes) in one big Float32Array. The "Skip 10 s" button fast-forwards the deaths and births of particles without timing them; it scrambles the free list the same way as letting time run. A C++ or Burst build would be faster overall, and your CPU's cache sizes decide where the jump happens, but the ratio is the lesson. In Lesson 005 mode, a particle is 16 floats (64 bytes): one Float32Array with a stride of 16 (AoS), 16 separate Float32Arrays, or 5 grouped ones (SoA). The "Loaded" and "Useful" numbers are counted exactly from the layout, not measured; the times are measured.
